h1: Spice Level 101: How Hot Are Bakudan's Spicy Bowls, Really?
meta_description: Deciding whether to order a spicy bowl at Bakudan Ramen? Here's a practical, comparative guide to Spicy Umami Miso, Spicy Shoyu, and Spice Bombs.
supporting_keywords: spicy umami miso vs spicy shoyu
audience: People unsure how much heat to order
image_alt: A bowl of Spicy Umami Miso ramen at Bakudan Ramen
body_html:
"How spicy is it" is one of the most common questions before ordering a spicy bowl anywhere, and it's a fair one — spice tolerance varies a lot person to person, and menu descriptions don't always translate into what you'll actually experience. Here's a practical comparison across Bakudan's heat-forward options.

Spicy Umami Miso

Built on a rich pork broth with a miso base, chili oil, and chili paste. The richness of the pork and miso base carries some of the heat, so it reads as bold and warming rather than sharp.

Spicy Shoyu

A chicken shoyu base with chili threads and togarashi. This one leans lighter overall than Spicy Umami Miso since it's chicken-broth-based rather than pork, but the chili threads and togarashi still bring real heat on top of that lighter base.

If Neither Sounds Right

Every bowl on the Ramen menu — including the milder ones like Bakudan Chicken or Vegetarian — can take a Spice Bomb, priced at $0.75 each. That means you don't have to choose between a mild broth and heat; you can start mild and add exactly as much as you want.

If You're Not Sure Where to Start

Ordering a milder bowl and adding one Spice Bomb is a lower-risk way to test your tolerance than jumping straight into Spicy Umami Miso or Spicy Shoyu at full intensity. You can always order those bowls outright on a future visit once you know where your tolerance actually sits.

There's No Penalty for Going Mild

Plenty of regulars order Bakudan Chicken or Cilantro Lime Chicken every time and never touch the spicy bowls or a Spice Bomb. Heat isn't a measure of how "serious" your order is — it's just a preference.
